ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Eisenmenger syndrome is the irreversible reversal of a long‑standing left‑to‑right shunt to right‑to‑left due to pulmonary hypertension, producing cyanosis and right‑heart failure.

sections.p: A chronic left‑to‑right shunt (often VSD, ASD, PDA) that, after years of pulmonary overcirculation, leads to pulmonary hypertension and shunt reversal. Diagnosis requires evidence of cyanosis, right‑heart strain, and a reversed shunt on imaging.
b: Reversed shunt on cardiac MRI or echo

sections.p: Staging follows WHO functional class and pulmonary pressure ranges, guiding prognosis and transplant candidacy.
Congenital defects that create a large left‑to‑right shunt are the primary culprits. In low‑resource settings, infections and conditions that raise pulmonary pressures can accelerate progression.
Patients develop progressive cyanosis, clubbing, exertional dyspnea, and right‑heart failure symptoms. Early signs may be subtle and mimic other conditions.
Key tests confirm shunt reversal, quantify pulmonary pressures, and assess right‑heart function. When resources are limited, clinical signs and basic imaging guide management.
Acute right‑heart failure, arrhythmias, thromboembolism, and sudden death are life‑threatening complications.

Treat the underlying cause if possible, provide supportive care, and prepare for lung transplantation when indicated. Pharmacologic choices aim to lower pulmonary pressures without worsening right‑heart failure.
Regular monitoring of oxygen saturation, right‑heart function, and pulmonary pressures is essential. Prevention focuses on early detection and repair of congenital shunts.
b: Referral for surgical repair before pulmonary hypertension develops

sections.p: Other cyanotic heart diseases and pulmonary hypertension causes can mimic Eisenmenger.
Normal chest X-ray or mild echo findings may mask severe pulmonary hypertension; low SpO2 can be misinterpreted as lung disease.
